evidence_claims.passage: **Human harvest:** A mature colony keeps a working surplus beyond what it needs to survive a bloom gap; that surplus, concentrated in the outer/newer storage cells, can be removed without touching the older, deeper cells the colony actually depends on — meaning a colony can be harvested from repeatedly across a season if a person takes only the outer surplus and leaves the core untouched. Destroying the whole nest for a one-time haul is easier but ends the relationship; leaving it standing rewards a return visit next season, which is the likely origin of "managed wild colony" behavior — people learning which hollow trunks host productive colonies and returning to them rather than raiding indiscriminately

evidence_claims.passage: - **Basingrazer (018)** and **Plateauhorn (019)** — both ruled out: 2.5–3 tonnes, matriarchal megaherds built around outrunning nothing and fighting everything. Too large to feed, house, or restrain with pre-agricultural tools, and their defense strategy (stand and fight with horns/head-shield) doesn't de-escalate around humans the way domestication needs. - **Thicketback (012)** — considered: right size range (300–400kg), but its defense is scatter-and-freeze in dense cover, and its small family bands don't generalize a stable dominance hierarchy a human could step into. Better fit for a future small-livestock candidate than a pack/milk animal.

evidence_claims.passage: **Writer-facing description:** A Goldbloom grove in bloom sounds wrong before it sounds anything else — no droning hum overhead, just a constant papery rustle of wings taking short, deliberate hops from flower to flower along the same branch. evidence_claims.passage: **Human harvest:** A mature colony keeps a working surplus beyond what it needs to survive a bloom gap; that surplus, concentrated in the outer/newer storage cells, can be removed without touching the older, deeper cells the colony actually depends on — meaning a colony can be harvested from repeatedly across a season if a person takes only the outer surplus and leaves the core untouched. Destroying the whole nest for a one-time haul is easier but ends the relationship; leaving it standing rewards a return visit next season, which is the likely origin of "managed wild colony" behavior — people learning which hollow trunks host productive colonies and returning to them rather than raiding indiscriminately

evidence_claims.passage: - **Basingrazer (018)** and **Plateauhorn (019)** — both ruled out: 2.5–3 tonnes, matriarchal megaherds built around outrunning nothing and fighting everything. Too large to feed, house, or restrain with pre-agricultural tools, and their defense strategy (stand and fight with horns/head-shield) doesn't de-escalate around humans the way domestication needs. - **Thicketback (012)** — considered: right size range (300–400kg), but its defense is scatter-and-freeze in dense cover, and its small family bands don't generalize a stable dominance hierarchy a human could step into. Better fit for a future small-livestock candidate than a pack/milk animal.

evidence_claims.passage: **Human harvest:** A mature colony keeps a working surplus beyond what it needs to survive a bloom gap; that surplus, concentrated in the outer/newer storage cells, can be removed without touching the older, deeper cells the colony actually depends on — meaning a colony can be harvested from repeatedly across a season if a person takes only the outer surplus and leaves the core untouched. Destroying the whole nest for a one-time haul is easier but ends the relationship; leaving it standing rewards a return visit next season, which is the likely origin of "managed wild colony" behavior — people learning which hollow trunks host productive colonies and returning to them rather than raiding indiscriminately

Destroying the whole nest for a one-time haul is easier but ends the relationship; leaving it standing rewards a return visit next season, which is the likely origin of "managed wild colony" behavior — people learning which hollow trunks host productive colonies and returning to them rather than raiding indiscriminately

Destroying the whole nest for a one-time haul is easier but ends the relationship; leaving it standing rewards a return visit next season, which is the likely origin of "managed wild colony" behavior — people learning which hollow trunks host productive colonies and returning to them rather than raiding indiscriminately

evidence_claims.passage: **Human harvest:** A mature colony keeps a working surplus beyond what it needs to survive a bloom gap; that surplus, concentrated in the outer/newer storage cells, can be removed without touching the older, deeper cells the colony actually depends on — meaning a colony can be harvested from repeatedly across a season if a person takes only the outer surplus and leaves the core untouched. Destroying the whole nest for a one-time haul is easier but ends the relationship; leaving it standing rewards a return visit next season, which is the likely origin of "managed wild colony" behavior — people learning which hollow trunks host productive colonies and returning to them rather than raiding indiscriminately

evidence_claims.passage: **Human harvest:** A mature colony keeps a working surplus beyond what it needs to survive a bloom gap; that surplus, concentrated in the outer/newer storage cells, can be removed without touching the older, deeper cells the colony actually depends on — meaning a colony can be harvested from repeatedly across a season if a person takes only the outer surplus and leaves the core untouched. evidence_quality.passage: **Human harvest:** A mature colony keeps a working surplus beyond what it needs to survive a bloom gap; that surplus, concentrated in the outer/newer storage cells, can be removed without touching the older, deeper cells the colony actually depends on — meaning a colony can be harvested from repeatedly across a season if a person takes only the outer surplus and leaves the core untouched. evidence_claims.passage: **Human harvest:** A mature colony keeps a working surplus beyond what it needs to survive a bloom gap; that surplus, concentrated in the outer/newer storage cells, can be removed without touching the older, deeper cells the colony actually depends on — meaning a colony can be harvested from repeatedly across a season if a person takes only the outer surplus and leaves the core untouched. Destroying the whole nest for a one-time haul is easier but ends the relationship; leaving it standing rewards a return visit next season, which is the likely origin of "managed wild colony" behavior — people learning which hollow trunks host productive colonies and returning to them rather than raiding indiscriminately

evidence_quality.passage: **Human harvest:** A mature colony keeps a working surplus beyond what it needs to survive a bloom gap; that surplus, concentrated in the outer/newer storage cells, can be removed without touching the older, deeper cells the colony actually depends on — meaning a colony can be harvested from repeatedly across a season if a person takes only the outer surplus and leaves the core untouched. evidence_claims.passage: **Human harvest:** A mature colony keeps a working surplus beyond what it needs to survive a bloom gap; that surplus, concentrated in the outer/newer storage cells, can be removed without touching the older, deeper cells the colony actually depends on — meaning a colony can be harvested from repeatedly across a season if a person takes only the outer surplus and leaves the core untouched. Destroying the whole nest for a one-time haul is easier but ends the relationship; leaving it standing rewards a return visit next season, which is the likely origin of "managed wild colony" behavior — people learning which hollow trunks host productive colonies and returning to them rather than raiding indiscriminately

Better fit for a future small-livestock candidate than a pack/milk animal.

evidence_claims.passage: **Human harvest:** A mature colony keeps a working surplus beyond what it needs to survive a bloom gap; that surplus, concentrated in the outer/newer storage cells, can be removed without touching the older, deeper cells the colony actually depends on — meaning a colony can be harvested from repeatedly across a season if a person takes only the outer surplus and leaves the core untouched. Destroying the whole nest for a one-time haul is easier but ends the relationship; leaving it standing rewards a return visit next season, which is the likely origin of "managed wild colony" behavior — people learning which hollow trunks host productive colonies and returning to them rather than raiding indiscriminately

evidence_claims.passage: **Human harvest:** A mature colony keeps a working surplus beyond what it needs to survive a bloom gap; that surplus, concentrated in the outer/newer storage cells, can be removed without touching the older, deeper cells the colony actually depends on — meaning a colony can be harvested from repeatedly across a season if a person takes only the outer surplus and leaves the core untouched. Destroying the whole nest for a one-time haul is easier but ends the relationship; leaving it standing rewards a return visit next season, which is the likely origin of "managed wild colony" behavior — people learning which hollow trunks host productive colonies and returning to them rather than raiding indiscriminately

evidence_claims.passage: **Human harvest:** A mature colony keeps a working surplus beyond what it needs to survive a bloom gap; that surplus, concentrated in the outer/newer storage cells, can be removed without touching the older, deeper cells the colony actually depends on — meaning a colony can be harvested from repeatedly across a season if a person takes only the outer surplus and leaves the core untouched. Destroying the whole nest for a one-time haul is easier but ends the relationship; leaving it standing rewards a return visit next season, which is the likely origin of "managed wild colony" behavior — people learning which hollow trunks host productive colonies and returning to them rather than raiding indiscriminately
